nameStory: The 'Clava' part of this hydrozoan's name comes from the Latin word for 'club,' referring to its club-shaped polyps. The species name 'multicornis' means 'many-horned,' describing the numerous tentacle-like projections that emerge from each polyp like tiny horns.
description: The club hydroid is a small colonial marine animal that looks like a tiny underwater forest of club-shaped tubes. Each individual polyp stands about 1-3mm tall and is topped with a ring of delicate tentacles. These creatures are hydrozoans, which are relatives of jellyfish and sea anemones, but they live attached to hard surfaces in shallow coastal waters. The colonies can spread across several inches of surface area.

idTips.label: Club-shaped polyps
idTips.description: Individual polyps have a distinctive swollen, club-like shape that's wider at the top than the base, making them look like tiny bowling pins topped with tentacles

idTips.label: Tentacle arrangement
idTips.description: Each polyp has 15-20 thin tentacles arranged in a neat circle around the mouth, looking like a delicate crown when viewed from above

idTips.label: Colonial growth
idTips.description: Forms spreading colonies connected by thin runners along the surface, creating patches that feel slightly slimy to the touch when exposed at low tide

idTips.label: Attachment surface
idTips.description: Always found growing on hard surfaces like rocks, shells, or pier pilings, never on sand or mud

idTips.label: Size and texture
idTips.description: Polyps are tiny (1-3mm) but visible to the naked eye, with a soft, translucent appearance that looks almost glass-like when submerged

habitat: Club hydroids attach to hard surfaces in shallow marine waters along New England's rocky coastlines. Look for them on rocks, shells, dock pilings, and other solid substrates in the intertidal zone and shallow subtidal areas. They prefer areas with good water circulation and are often found alongside barnacles, mussels, and other encrusting marine life.

seasonality.spring: Colonies begin active growth as water temperatures rise, with new polyps budding from the colonial runners. This is when they're most easily spotted as they expand their coverage.
seasonality.summer: Peak season for observation, with fully developed colonies displaying their characteristic club-shaped polyps and active feeding behavior when submerged.
seasonality.fall: Colonies remain active but may begin to show signs of seasonal die-back in colder areas. Still readily identifiable on hard substrates.
seasonality.winter: Can enter dormancy during harsh conditions, with some polyps retracting or dying back, though the colonial base often survives to regrow in spring.

funFact: Despite being barely visible to the naked eye, club hydroid larvae have remarkably advanced nervous systems for their tiny size - they're like microscopic underwater geniuses with better neural networks than many much larger animals!
confusionNotes: Club hydroids can be confused with other small colonial hydroids, but their distinctive club shape sets them apart from the more tube-like or branching forms of relatives. Remember: if it looks like tiny clubs with tentacle crowns, you've found Clava multicornis.
contextualKnowledge: This species has had many different scientific names over the years (including Hydra multicornis and Coryne squamata), so you might see it listed under various names in older field guides. Despite the name similarities, these marine hydroids are completely unrelated to the freshwater hydras often studied in biology classes.
compareHints: Clava multicornis is the only species in its genus, making it unique among New England hydroids for its club-shaped polyps. Other hydroid species in the family tend to have more cylindrical or branching growth forms, while Clava's distinctive swollen, club-like polyps with their neat rings of tentacles are unmistakable once you know what to look for.
